title: The 80/20 Principle
summary: 80% of results come from 20% of efforts. Identify the vital few inputs that produce the majority of your outcomes, and focus there. The rest is noise.
source: The 80/20 Principle by Richard Koch

title: Stoicism — The Dichotomy of Control
summary: Some things are within your control, others are not. Your opinions, actions, and desires — yes. Your reputation, wealth, and what others think — no. Peace comes from focusing only on what you can control.
source: Epictetus, Enchiridion

title: Entropy — The Arrow of Time
summary: The Second Law of Thermodynamics says entropy (disorder) always increases. That's why eggs scramble but never unscramble, and why time only moves forward. The universe is slowly running down.
source: The Order of Time by Carlo Rovelli

title: Start With Why
summary: People don't buy what you do, they buy why you do it. Great leaders and organizations — Apple, MLK, the Wright brothers — all think, act, and communicate from the inside out: Why → How → What.
source: Simon Sinek, TEDxPugetSound

title: The 4-Hour Workweek — Lifestyle Design
summary: Retirement is a worst-case-scenario insurance plan. Design your life now. Outsource, automate, and eliminate. Focus on 'what would you do if you had a million dollars?' — then find a way to do it today.
source: The 4-Hour Workweek by Tim Ferriss

title: The Myth of Sisyphus
summary: Life is absurd — we seek meaning in a universe that offers none. Camus's answer: embrace the absurd. Imagine Sisyphus happy. The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart.
source: The Myth of Sisyphus by Albert Camus

title: Photosynthesis — Electrons from Sunlight
summary: Plants split water using sunlight, grabbing electrons to turn CO₂ into sugar. It's the most efficient solar panel on Earth — and the foundation of almost all life. Without it, there's no oxygen, no food, no us.
source: What Is Life? by Nick Lane

title: The Power of Vulnerability
summary: Vulnerability isn't weakness — it's the birthplace of connection, courage, and creativity. To be vulnerable is to show up and be seen, even when there are no guarantees. You cannot numb shame without numbing joy.
source: Brené Brown, TEDxHouston

title: Atomic Habits — 1% Better Every Day
summary: Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement. Tiny changes → remarkable results. Focus on systems, not goals. Make good habits obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying. Your identity is your habits.
source: Atomic Habits by James Clear

title: The Trolley Problem
summary: A runaway trolley is heading toward five people. You can pull a lever to divert it onto a side track, killing one person instead. Is it moral to act? This thought experiment exposes the tension between utilitarian ethics (save the most lives) and deontological ethics (don't intentionally harm).
source: Philippa Foot / Judith Jarvis Thomson

title: Quantum Tunneling — Walking Through Walls
summary: At the quantum scale, particles can pass through barriers they seemingly shouldn't be able to cross. This isn't magic — it's probability. Your computer's transistors and the Sun's nuclear fusion both depend on quantum tunneling.
source: Quantum: A Guide for the Perplexed by Jim Al-Khalili

title: Grit — Passion and Perseverance
summary: Talent doesn't make you gritty. Grit is passion and perseverance for long-term goals. It's living life like a marathon, not a sprint. The gritty ones stick with their future, day in, day out — and that's what separates achievers from the rest.
source: Angela Duckworth, TED Talk

title: Rich Dad Poor Dad — Assets vs Liabilities
summary: The rich buy assets. The poor and middle class buy liabilities they think are assets. An asset puts money in your pocket. A liability takes money out. Build your asset column until it can cover your expenses. Then you're free.
source: Rich Dad Poor Dad by Robert Kiyosaki

title: The Veil of Ignorance
summary: Imagine designing a society without knowing your place in it — your gender, race, wealth, or talents. Behind this 'veil of ignorance,' you'd create a fair system because you could end up anywhere. That's justice as fairness.
source: A Theory of Justice by John Rawls

title: The Observable Universe
summary: The universe is 93 billion light-years across, but we can only see what's within the observable horizon — about 13.8 billion years old. The light from beyond hasn't had time to reach us. And the universe is expanding faster every day.
source: Astrophysics for People in a Hurry by Neil deGrasse Tyson

title: How Schools Kill Creativity
summary: Creativity is as important as literacy, and schools systematically educate it out of children. We're taught to be afraid of being wrong. But if you're not prepared to be wrong, you'll never come up with anything original.
source: Sir Ken Robinson, TED Talk

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
summary: You have two systems of thought: System 1 is fast, intuitive, emotional. System 2 is slow, deliberate, logical. System 1 runs your life most of the time. It's efficient but prone to biases. Knowing when to slow down is wisdom.
source: Thinking, Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman

title: Plato's Allegory of the Cave
summary: Prisoners chained in a cave see only shadows on the wall and believe that's reality. One escapes, sees the sun (truth), and returns to free the others — who reject him. Education is painful enlightenment. Most people prefer the shadows.
source: The Republic by Plato

title: Your Brain Forgets on Purpose
summary: Forgetting isn't a bug — it's a feature. Your brain prunes unused connections to make room for what matters. Sleep is when your brain consolidates memories and clears metabolic waste. That's why pulling all-nighters backfires.
source: Why We Sleep by Matthew Walker

title: The Happy Secret to Better Work
summary: Your brain works better when positive. Happiness isn't a destination you get to after success — it's the fuel for success itself. 'The Harvard Business Review' reports a 31% productivity increase in a positive brain. Dopamine = performance.
source: Shawn Achor, TEDxBloomington

title: Digital Minimalism
summary: You don't need to quit social media entirely. You need to adopt a philosophy of technology use: spend your time and attention on a small number of carefully chosen activities that strongly serve your values, and miss out on everything else.
source: Digital Minimalism by Cal Newport

title: Nietzsche — God is Dead
summary: Nietzsche didn't celebrate the death of God — he warned us. Without a divine moral framework, humanity must create its own values. Most people will crumble under this freedom. The Übermensch forges their own meaning from the abyss.
source: Thus Spoke Zarathustra by Friedrich Nietzsche

title: Natural Selection — Survival of the Fittest
summary: Not the biggest or the smartest survive — the most adaptable. Small genetic variations give some individuals a slight edge. Over millions of years, these tiny advantages compound into entirely new species. Evolution is a tinkerer, not an engineer.
source: The Selfish Gene by Richard Dawkins

title: Fake It Till You Become It
summary: Your body language shapes who you are. Holding 'power poses' for two minutes increases testosterone and decreases cortisol. Your brain takes cues from your posture. Stand like a winner long enough, and you become one.
source: Amy Cuddy, TED Talk

title: Freakonomics — Incentives Rule the World
summary: People respond to incentives, even when they don't realize it. Sumo wrestlers cheat. Real estate agents sell your house for less. The Ku Klux Klan was dismantled by a comic book. Follow the incentives and you'll understand human behavior.
source: Freakonomics by Steven Levitt & Stephen Dubner

title: The Tao — Effortless Action
summary: Wu Wei (non-action) doesn't mean doing nothing. It means acting in perfect alignment with the natural flow, like water. Water never fights — it flows around obstacles, wears down stone, and always finds the lowest place. Be like water.
source: Tao Te Ching by Lao Tzu

title: The Fibonacci Sequence in Nature
summary: 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21… This simple number sequence appears everywhere in nature: sunflower seed spirals, pinecones, nautilus shells, and even galaxy arms. It's the universe's favorite pattern for efficient packing.
source: The Golden Ratio by Mario Livio

title: The Pale Blue Dot
summary: Every human who ever lived — all their wars, loves, triumphs, and failures — happened on a 'mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.' From 4 billion miles away, Earth is a pale blue dot. This perspective is humbling. Look after each other.
source: Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot

title: Meditations — Memento Mori
summary: Marcus Aurelius wrote to himself: 'You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think.' Remember you will die (memento mori). Not as a morbid thought — as a compass. It strips away the trivial.
source: Meditations by Marcus Aurelius

title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness
summary: We know how the brain processes information (the easy problems). But why does it feel like something to be you? Why is there subjective experience at all? The 'hard problem' remains unsolved — and may be the deepest mystery in the universe.
source: Consciousness Explained by Daniel Dennett

title: The Miller-Urey Experiment
summary: In 1953, scientists simulated early Earth — lightning sparks through a mix of methane, ammonia, and water. Within days, amino acids formed spontaneously. The building blocks of life aren't rare. They're an inevitable chemical reaction.
source: The Vital Question by Nick Lane

title: Inside the Writer's Mind
summary: Writing isn't about having great ideas — it's about showing up every day. The gap between your taste and your ability is painful. Close it by producing work, failing, learning, and producing again. Don't wait for inspiration. Build the habit.
source: Ira Glass, This American Life

title: Never Split the Difference
summary: In negotiation, splitting the difference is a coward's move. Use calibrated questions ('How am I supposed to do that?') and mirroring (repeat the last few words). People want to be heard and understood — that's your leverage. Not logic.
source: Never Split the Difference by Chris Voss

title: The Golden Mean
summary: Aristotle said virtue lies between two vices — excess and deficiency. Courage is between cowardice and recklessness. Generosity sits between miserliness and wastefulness. There's no formula. The golden mean is wisdom from lived experience.
source: Nicomachean Ethics by Aristotle

title: Machine Learning — Learning from Data
summary: Instead of programming rules, we give AI examples. A neural network adjusts millions of internal parameters until it can recognize patterns it has never seen. It's not magic — it's statistics on steroids, trained on massive datasets.
source: The Alignment Problem by Brian Christian

title: The Danger of a Single Story
summary: If you only hear one story about a person or a country, you risk a critical misunderstanding. A single story creates stereotypes. The problem with stereotypes is not that they're untrue — it's that they're incomplete. The single story robs people of dignity.
source: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, TED Talk

title: The Fifth Discipline — Systems Thinking
summary: Most problems are interconnected systems, not isolated events. Fixing symptoms without understanding the system creates worse problems. The beer game, the arms race, even your diet — they all loop back on themselves. See the whole system.
source: The Fifth Discipline by Peter Senge

title: Determinism vs Free Will
summary: If every event has a cause, and your choices are caused by prior events you didn't choose, is free will an illusion? Compatibilists say freedom is acting according to your own desires — even if those desires are determined. Hard determinists say it's all an illusion.
source: Free Will by Sam Harris

title: Tectonic Plates — Earth's Moving Crust
summary: Earth's outer shell is cracked into 15-20 plates floating on molten rock. They move about as fast as your fingernails grow — but over millions of years, they build mountains, create oceans, and cause earthquakes. The Himalayas are still rising 5mm/year.
source: Earth: An Intimate History by Richard Fortey

title: The Power of Boredom
summary: Constant stimulation destroys your ability to focus. Boredom is the training ground for deep thinking. When you're bored, your brain enters the default mode network — where creative connections happen. Don't reach for your phone. Sit with it.
source: Manoush Zomorodi, TED Radio Hour

title: Influence — The Weapons of Persuasion
summary: Six principles drive human compliance: reciprocity (give first), scarcity (limited time), authority (expert status), consistency (commitments), liking (similarity), and social proof (everyone's doing it). Know them to defend against them.
source: Influence by Robert Cialdini

title: Buddhism — The Four Noble Truths
summary: 1) Life involves suffering. 2) Suffering comes from attachment and craving. 3) It's possible to end suffering. 4) The Eightfold Path leads there: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration.
source: What the Buddha Taught by Walpola Rahula

title: Antibiotics vs Viruses — The Difference
summary: Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses. Bacteria are living cells. Viruses are just genetic material in a protein coat — they can't reproduce without hijacking your cells. That's why antibiotics don't work on the common cold. Don't misuse them.
source: I Contain Multitudes by Ed Yong

title: The Power of Yet
summary: A teacher who tells a struggling student 'You can't do it' vs 'You can't do it yet' changes everything. The word 'yet' creates a growth mindset — the belief that ability can be developed. Praise effort, not intelligence.
source: Carol Dweck, TEDx Talk

title: How to Win Friends — The Shortcut
summary: The fastest way to influence someone: become genuinely interested in them. A person's name is the sweetest sound in any language. Talk about what they want and show them how to get it. Criticize indirectly. Let them save face.
source: How to Win Friends and Influence People by Dale Carnegie

title: Walden — Simplify, Simplify
summary: Thoreau went to the woods to live deliberately — to front only the essential facts of life. Most people live lives of quiet desperation burdened by possessions they don't need. Simplify. Reduce. The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
source: Walden by Henry David Thoreau

title: Lucy — The 3.2 Million Year Old Fossil
summary: In 1974, a 40% complete female hominid skeleton was found in Ethiopia. Lucy walked upright but had a small brain. She proved that bipedalism came before big brains. Our ancestors stood up before they got smart. Walking changed everything.
source: The Story of the Human Body by Daniel Lieberman

title: Speak Like a Leader
summary: Great speakers don't use complex language. They use short words, short sentences, and pregnant pauses. Silence is powerful — it signals confidence. And the most persuasive sound in any language? Silence after an important point.
source: Julian Treasure, TED Talk

title: Zero to One — Monopoly is Good
summary: Capitalism and competition are opposites. Competition destroys profits. Every great business is a monopoly — it does something so well that no one else can compete. The best companies create entirely new categories (0 to 1), not copy existing ones (1 to n).
source: Zero to One by Peter Thiel

title: Occam's Razor — The Simplest Explanation
summary: When faced with competing explanations, the one with the fewest assumptions is usually correct. Not because simplicity is always right — but because explanations with fewer assumptions are less likely to be wrong. Don't multiply entities beyond necessity.
source: Philosophical investigations by Bertrand Russell

title: Flow — The Optimal Experience
summary: Flow is the state of complete absorption in an activity — losing yourself in the moment. It happens when challenge matches skill. Time dilates, self-consciousness vanishes, and the activity becomes intrinsically rewarding. Happiness is flow, not leisure.
source: Flow by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi

title: Sartre — We Are Condemned to Be Free
summary: Existence precedes essence. You aren't born with a purpose — you create one through your choices. There's no human nature to fall back on. You are totally free, and totally responsible. 'Man is condemned to be free; because having created himself, he is entirely responsible for everything he does.'
source: Being and Nothingness by Jean-Paul Sartre

title: Special Relativity — Time is Relative
summary: Einstein showed that time slows down the faster you move. At 99% of light speed, one year on a spaceship could equal decades on Earth. This isn't science fiction — GPS satellites have to correct for relativity every day or they'd be off by kilometers.
source: Einstein: His Life and Universe by Walter Isaacson

title: The Story of Stuff
summary: Our economy is a linear system (take-make-dispose) on a finite planet. Every stage — extraction, production, distribution, consumption, disposal — has hidden costs. The average American consumes twice their body weight in materials daily. This isn't sustainable.
source: Annie Leonard, The Story of Stuff

title: Deep Work — The Superpower of the 21st Century
summary: Deep work is professionally valuable, rare, and becoming rarer. Shallow work (email, slack, meetings) feels productive but isn't. Schedule deep work blocks. Quit social media. Embrace boredom. The ability to concentrate without distraction is becoming the new IQ.
source: Deep Work by Cal Newport

title: The Greatest Happiness Principle
summary: Actions are right if they promote happiness, wrong if they produce the opposite. Utilitarianism asks you to consider the greatest good for the greatest number — including animals (they can suffer too). The catch: who decides what 'good' means?
source: Utilitarianism by John Stuart Mill

title: Neutron Stars — Cosmic Lighthouses
summary: When a massive star collapses, its core compresses into a ball of neutrons the size of a city — but with the mass of the Sun. A teaspoon of neutron star weighs a billion tons. Some spin 700 times per second, emitting beams of radiation like cosmic lighthouses.
source: Death by Black Hole by Neil deGrasse Tyson

title: The Invisible Gorilla
summary: Half the participants in a famous experiment failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walk through a basketball game — because they were counting passes. When you focus intently on one thing, you miss the obvious. This is inattentional blindness, and it happens daily.
source: Christopher Chabris & Daniel Simons, TED Talk

title: Nudge — The Gentle Push
summary: Small changes in how choices are presented can dramatically change behavior. Default options are powerful — opt-out organ donation vs opt-in. Cafeterias that put fruit at eye level sell more fruit. Libertarian paternalism: preserve freedom while steering good decisions.
source: Nudge by Richard Thaler & Cass Sunstein

title: Zen — The Beginner's Mind
summary: In the beginner's mind there are many possibilities, in the expert's mind there are few. Shoshin — approaching every experience as if for the first time — opens the door to genuine understanding. Drop your preconceptions. The freshest view is often the truest.
source: Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind by Shunryu Suzuki

title: Mitochondria — The Powerhouse
summary: Every cell in your body contains hundreds of mitochondria — tiny organelles that convert food into ATP, the energy currency of life. They have their own DNA (inherited from your mother) and were once free-living bacteria. Without them, you'd be dead in seconds.
source: The Vital Question by Nick Lane

title: How Language Shapes Thought
summary: The language you speak affects how you think. Speakers of languages without future tense (like Finnish) save more for retirement — the future feels closer. Speakers of languages with absolute directions (north/south instead of left/right) have extraordinary navigational abilities.
source: Lera Boroditsky, TED Talk

title: The Hero's Journey
summary: Every great story follows the same pattern: a hero leaves their ordinary world, crosses a threshold into adventure, faces trials, wins a victory, and returns transformed. From Star Wars to Harry Potter to The Lord of the Rings — the monomyth is universal.
source: The Hero with a Thousand Faces by Joseph Campbell

title: Epicureanism — The Art of Simple Pleasures
summary: Epicurus didn't advocate for wild hedonism — he taught that the highest pleasure is a life of simple moderation, friendship, and freedom from fear. A meal of bread and water shared with friends can be as satisfying as a feast. Fear of death is the greatest obstacle to happiness.
source: The Art of Happiness by Epicurus

title: Neuroplasticity — Your Brain Rewires Itself
summary: Your brain isn't fixed after childhood — it rewires itself throughout life. London taxi drivers have larger hippocampi (memory centers) from memorizing streets. Stroke patients can retrain other brain regions to take over. You can literally change your brain by changing what you do.
source: The Brain That Changes Itself by Norman Doidge

title: The Most Astounding Fact
summary: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old. Our bodies are made of elements forged in stars that exploded billions of years ago. The nitrogen in our DNA, the calcium in our bones, the iron in our blood — all cooked in the heart of a star. We are literally stardust.
source: Neil deGrasse Tyson, TIME Talk

title: Good to Great — The Hedgehog Concept
summary: Great companies focus on one thing they can be the best in the world at, that drives their economic engine, and that they're passionate about. This three-circle Venn diagram is the Hedgehog Concept. Foxes know many things; hedgehogs know one big thing.
source: Good to Great by Jim Collins

title: The Ship of Theseus
summary: If you replace every plank of a ship over time, is it still the same ship? What if you reassemble the old planks into a second ship — which one is the original? This ancient paradox questions identity itself. Are you still the same person you were 10 years ago?
source: Plutarch, Parallel Lives

title: The Neanderthal in Your DNA
summary: If you're of non-African descent, about 2% of your DNA comes from Neanderthals. Modern humans interbred with Neanderthals 50,000 years ago. Those ancient genes affect your immune system, skin, and even your risk for depression and blood clots. Your ancestors met and mingled.
source: Who We Are and How We Got Here by David Reich

title: The Next Web — The Semantic Web
summary: The internet is growing beyond documents. We're entering an era where machines can understand the meaning (semantics) of information — not just display it. Imagine an AI that can read every medical paper, cross-reference your symptoms, and tell your doctor what's wrong. That future is being built now.
source: Tim Berners-Lee, TED Talk

title: Emotional Intelligence Matters More Than IQ
summary: IQ gets you hired; EQ gets you promoted. Emotional intelligence — self-awareness, empathy, self-regulation, social skills — is a better predictor of success than raw intelligence. The most effective leaders aren't the smartest in the room; they're the most attuned to the room.
source: Emotional Intelligence by Daniel Goleman

title: The Second Sex — One is Not Born a Woman
summary: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. Gender is a social construct layered onto biological sex. Throughout history, woman has been defined as the Other — secondary to man. Freedom requires refusing to be defined by anyone else's categories.
source: The Second Sex by Simone de Beauvoir

title: Graphene — The Miracle Material
summary: Graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms, one atom thick — yet 200 times stronger than steel. It conducts electricity better than copper and heat better than diamond. It's flexible, transparent, and almost impermeable. It could revolutionize batteries, electronics, and water filters.
source: The Physics of Superheroes by James Kakalios

title: Science is a Way of Thinking
summary: Science isn't a body of facts — it's a method of thinking. Question everything. Demand evidence. Be willing to be wrong. The scientific method is the most powerful tool humanity has ever created. But it only works if you follow the evidence wherever it leads, even when uncomfortable.
source: Carl Sagan, The Demon-Haunted World

title: The Cue-Routine-Reward Loop
summary: Every habit follows a neurological loop: cue (trigger), routine (action), reward (benefit). To change a habit, keep the same cue and reward — just change the routine. Want to stop stress-eating? Keep the cue (stress) and reward (satisfaction), but swap the routine (eat → walk).
source: The Power of Habit by Charles Duhigg

title: The Social Contract
summary: Society is an agreement we all make: give up some freedom in exchange for security and order. Rousseau said people are born free but are everywhere in chains. Hobbes argued that without government, life would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' The contract is what makes civilization possible.
source: The Social Contract by Jean-Jacques Rousseau

title: The Greenhouse Effect
summary: CO₂ and methane trap heat from the sun, keeping Earth 33°C warmer than it would be otherwise — that's a good thing. The problem is we've increased CO₂ by 50% since the Industrial Revolution. More greenhouse gas = more trapped heat = a planet that's warming dangerously fast.
source: The Uninhabitable Earth by David Wallace-Wells

title: The 20-Second Rule
summary: The biggest barrier to good habits isn't motivation — it's friction. Reduce the friction for good habits (keep running shoes by the door) and increase it for bad ones (put the TV remote in the basement). Shawn Achor calls this the 20-Second Rule: if a habit takes 20 more seconds of effort, you won't do it.
source: The Happiness Advantage by Shawn Achor

title: Antifragile — What Doesn't Kill You Makes You Stronger
summary: Some things benefit from shocks. Fragile things break under stress. Robust things resist stress. Antifragile things get stronger from stress — like the immune system, muscles, and startups. To thrive in chaos, build antifragility. Don't just survive uncertainty — profit from it.
source: Antifragile by Nassim Nicholas Taleb

title: The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
summary: If an autonomous car must choose between hitting five pedestrians or killing its passenger, who decides? As AI makes more decisions in our lives — loans, hiring, medicine, justice — we need ethical frameworks for machines. The trolley problem has become an engineering problem.
source: Superintelligence by Nick Bostrom

title: The Higgs Boson — Why Things Have Mass
summary: The Higgs field is an invisible energy field that permeates the universe. Particles gain mass by interacting with it — imagine moving through molasses. The Higgs boson, discovered in 2012, is the particle that proves the field exists. Without it, everything would be massless and flying at light speed.
source: The God Particle by Leon Lederman

title: Drive — What Motivates Us
summary: For creative work, carrot-and-stick doesn't work. What drives high performance: autonomy (control over your work), mastery (desire to get better), and purpose (a cause bigger than yourself). Companies that give employees 20% time (Google) or unlimited autonomy produce breakthrough innovation.
source: Daniel Pink, RSA Animate

title: The Power of Compound Interest
summary: Einstein called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world. Invest $10,000 at 8% annual return: in 30 years it becomes $100,000 without adding a cent. Start early. Time is the most powerful factor. The stock market has returned ~7% after inflation for over a century. Patience beats timing.
source: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing by John Bogle

title: The Socratic Method — Question Everything
summary: Socrates didn't teach answers — he asked questions. By relentlessly questioning assumptions, he exposed contradictions in people's beliefs. The goal isn't to win an argument but to arrive at truth. Asking 'Why?' five times in a row is still one of the most powerful tools for clear thinking.
source: The Republic by Plato (Socratic Dialogues)

title: Your Microbiome — The 2nd Brain
summary: Your body contains trillions of bacteria that outnumber your human cells 1.3 to 1. They digest food, produce vitamins, regulate your immune system, and even influence your mood. The gut-brain axis is real — 90% of your serotonin is produced in your gut. You are a walking ecosystem.
source: I Contain Multitudes by Ed Yong

title: Getting Things Done
summary: The gold standard for personal productivity. Capture everything in a trusted system outside your head. Clarify what each item means and decide the next action. Organize by context (calls, errands, at computer). Review weekly. Do it.
source: Getting Things Done by David Allen

title: The Coddling of the American Mind
summary: Three untruths have spread: what doesn't kill you makes you weaker (vs stronger), always trust your feelings (vs question them), and life is a battle between good and bad people (vs good and evil in everyone). These lead to fragility, not resilience.
source: The Coddling of the American Mind by Lukianoff & Haidt

title: Stumbling on Happiness
summary: Your brain is terrible at predicting what will make you happy. You think winning the lottery will make you happier forever - it won't. You think paralysis will make you miserable forever - it won't. The psychological immune system is powerful. You adapt to almost everything.
source: Stumbling on Happiness by Daniel Gilbert

title: Predictably Irrational
summary: Humans are not rational. We make the same mistakes over and over - predictably. Free is too powerful (people grab free stuff over better deals). We overvalue what we own (endowment effect). We compare everything relatively. Understand these patterns to outsmart yourself.
source: Predictably Irrational by Dan Ariely

title: Rework
summary: Meetings are toxic. Workaholism is a waste. Planning is guessing. Build half a product, not a half-assed product. Stay small. Ignore competition. Say no by default. You don't need a business plan, an office, or investors - you need to make something people want.
source: Rework by Jason Fried & DHH

title: Why We Sleep
summary: Sleep is the single most effective thing you can do to reset your brain and body. It boosts memory, regulates emotions, clears toxins, and strengthens your immune system. Routinely sleeping less than 6 hours increases cancer risk, Alzheimer's risk, and heart disease. Do not skimp on sleep.
source: Why We Sleep by Matthew Walker

title: The Emperor of All Maladies
summary: Cancer is not one disease - it's hundreds, each with different genetic drivers. We've spent decades waging war on it with poison (chemo), knives (surgery), and radiation. Only recently have targeted therapies and immunotherapy started to change the game. It's a story of hubris, hope, and incremental progress.
source: The Emperor of All Maladies by Siddhartha Mukherjee

title: The Elegant Universe
summary: String theory proposes that the fundamental building blocks of the universe are not particles but tiny vibrating strings. Different vibration patterns produce different particles - like musical notes. The theory requires 10 or 11 dimensions, most curled up so small we can't detect them. Elegant but unproven.
source: The Elegant Universe by Brian Greene

title: Cosmos
summary: The cosmos is all that is or ever was or ever will be. We are a way for the cosmos to know itself. Every atom in your body was forged in a star. The universe is vast - 100 billion galaxies, each with 100 billion stars. In the face of this scale, our problems seem small and our connection to each other profound.
source: Cosmos by Carl Sagan

title: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
summary: Science doesn't progress by accumulating facts - it progresses by revolutions. Normal science works within a paradigm until anomalies pile up. Then a crisis leads to a paradigm shift - a complete change in worldview (Copernicus, Darwin, Einstein). New paradigms are incommensurable with old ones.
source: The Structure of Scientific Revolutions by Thomas Kuhn

title: Outliers - The Story of Success
summary: No one succeeds alone. The 10,000-hour rule: true expertise requires roughly 10,000 hours of deliberate practice. But opportunity matters more - being born in the right year, having access to computers, growing up in a culture that values hard work. Bill Gates got 10,000 hours because his school had a terminal in 1968.
source: Outliers by Malcolm Gladwell

title: The Black Swan
summary: A Black Swan is a rare, high-impact event that seems predictable only in hindsight. 9/11, the 2008 financial crash, the rise of the internet - all were Black Swans. Most of history's biggest changes come from these unpredictable events. Stop pretending you can predict the future. Build robustness to the unknown.
source: The Black Swan by Nassim Nicholas Taleb

title: The Innovator's Dilemma
summary: Great companies fail not because they do things wrong - but because they do everything right. They listen to customers, invest in R&D, and optimize profits. Then a disruptive technology emerges that their customers don't want - yet. By the time it matters, the disruptor has taken over. The innovator's dilemma: doing the right thing leads to failure.
source: The Innovator's Dilemma by Clayton Christensen

title: Guns, Germs, and Steel
summary: Why did Europeans conquer the Americas and not the reverse? Not because of intelligence or genes - but geography. The East-West axis of Eurasia allowed crops and livestock to spread easily. Domesticated animals gave immunity to diseases that killed 95% of Native Americans. Geography is destiny.
source: Guns, Germs, and Steel by Jared Diamond

title: Sapiens - A Brief History of Humankind
summary: Homo sapiens conquered the world through three revolutions: Cognitive (language and fiction ~70k years ago), Agricultural (~12k years ago), and Scientific (~500 years ago). We're the only animal that cooperates flexibly in large numbers - because we believe in shared fictions like money, nations, and human rights.
source: Sapiens by Yuval Noah Harari

title: The One Thing
summary: What's the ONE thing you can do such that by doing it everything else will be easier or unnecessary? Extraordinary results come from narrowing your focus, not widening it. Multitasking is a lie. Willpower is a limited resource - do your most important work first. Protect your focus time like a meeting with the CEO.
source: The One Thing by Gary Keller

title: The Art of Thinking Clearly
summary: You are systematically delusional. You overestimate your own abilities (overconfidence bias). You see patterns in random noise (clustering illusion). You think things that just happened will happen again (recency bias). You believe what confirms what you already believe (confirmation bias). The first step: admit you're biased.
source: The Art of Thinking Clearly by Rolf Dobelli

title: The Gene - An Intimate History
summary: The gene is the unit of heredity - a stretch of DNA that codes for a protein. The Human Genome Project mapped all 20,000 of ours. We can now read, edit, and even synthesize genes. CRISPR lets us cure genetic diseases. But with this power comes hard questions: should we edit embryos? Choose our children's traits? Play God?
source: The Gene by Siddhartha Mukherjee

title: The Selfish Gene
summary: We are survival machines - vehicles for our genes. A gene's ultimate goal is to replicate itself, even at the expense of the organism. Altruism exists because helping relatives helps copies of your genes survive. Memes - ideas that spread like genes - are the next level of evolution. Dawkins changed how we think about evolution itself.
source: The Selfish Gene by Richard Dawkins

title: Attached - The Science of Attachment
summary: Your attachment style - anxious, avoidant, or secure - determines how you behave in relationships. Anxious types crave closeness and fear abandonment. Avoidant types value independence and fear intimacy. They attract each other (anxious-avoidant trap). Understanding your style is the key to better relationships.
source: Attached by Amir Levine & Rachel Heller

title: Essentialism - The Disciplined Pursuit of Less
summary: Essentialism is not about how to get more things done - it's about how to get the right things done. Less but better. If it's not a clear yes, it's a no. Trade-offs are real - you can't have it all. The essentialist does the right thing at the right time in the right way. Say no to almost everything.
source: Essentialism by Greg McKeown

title: Tiny Habits
summary: To build a habit, make it so small it's ridiculous. Floss one tooth. Do one pushup. Write one sentence. The smallness removes resistance. After the tiny behavior, celebrate - emotion creates habits, not repetition. Anchor new habits to existing ones. Small changes, wired by emotion, create lasting transformation.
source: Tiny Habits by BJ Fogg

title: Purple Cow - Stand Out or Be Invisible
summary: The old model: create a product, advertise it, sell it. That's dead. In a world of too many choices, remarkable products are the only marketing that works. Be a purple cow - something worth noticing, talking about, sharing. Safe is risky. Boring fails. Remarkable wins. If it's not remarkable, start over.
source: Purple Cow by Seth Godin

title: The Happiness Hypothesis
summary: Happiness is not something you find - it's something you create. The mind is divided: the rational rider and the emotional elephant. The rider thinks they're in control, but the elephant usually goes where it wants. To change, you need to speak to the elephant (emotion), not just the rider (logic).
source: The Happiness Hypothesis by Jonathan Haidt

title: Blue Ocean Strategy
summary: Don't compete in a bloody red ocean of rivals - create a blue ocean of uncontested market space. Cirque du Soleil didn't beat Ringling Bros; they combined circus and theater to create something entirely new. Value innovation - simultaneously pursue differentiation and low cost. Make the competition irrelevant.
source: Blue Ocean Strategy by W. Chan Kim

title: The Power of Now
summary: The present moment is all you ever have. The past is a memory; the future is an illusion. Psychological suffering comes from identifying with your mind - the voice in your head that's never satisfied. Watch your thoughts without judgment. Be present. When you're fully in the now, problems dissolve.
source: The Power of Now by Eckhart Tolle

title: Mastery
summary: Every master follows the same path: apprenticeship (learning the rules), creative-active (breaking the rules), and mastery (transcending the rules). It takes ~20 years. The key is finding your life's task - that childhood curiosity or obsession that won't go away. Combine deep practice with social intelligence.
source: Mastery by Robert Greene

title: The Lean Startup
summary: Startups aren't smaller versions of big companies - they're experiments. Build a Minimum Viable Product (MVP), measure how customers respond, learn, and pivot or persevere. The Build-Measure-Learn loop is the engine of growth. Stop building things nobody wants. Fail fast, learn faster.
source: The Lean Startup by Eric Ries

title: A Brief History of Time
summary: Spacetime curves around mass - that's gravity. Black holes are regions where gravity is so strong not even light escapes. The universe began as an infinitely dense singularity 13.8 billion years ago (Big Bang). It will end in heat death - maximum entropy. The universe has a beginning - and probably an end.
source: A Brief History of Time by Stephen Hawking

title: Skin in the Game
summary: Don't trust advice from someone who doesn't have skin in the game. If they're not risking something, their opinion is cheap. People who take risks learn from reality; people who don't learn from theory. Symmetry of risk is the foundation of fairness.
source: Skin in the Game by Nassim Nicholas Taleb

title: Pre-Suasion
summary: The best persuaders don't just deliver a great message - they create the right context before delivering it. What you present first changes how everything else is received. Pre-suade by setting the frame.
source: Pre-Suasion by Robert Cialdini

title: The Gifts of Imperfection
summary: Wholehearted living is about engaging in your life from a place of worthiness. You are enough - not despite your imperfections but because of them. Cultivate authenticity, self-compassion, and resilience. Let go of perfectionism, numbing, and what people think.
source: The Gifts of Imperfection by Brené Brown

title: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks
summary: HeLa cells - taken from Henrietta Lacks without her knowledge in 1951 - became the first immortal human cell line. They've been used for polio vaccines, cancer research, gene mapping, and COVID vaccines. Trillions of her cells exist today. It's a story of medical progress, racial injustice, and who owns your body.
source: The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks by Rebecca Skloot

title: The Miracle Morning
summary: How you start your morning sets the tone for your entire day. The SAVERS routine: Silence (meditation), Affirmations, Visualization, Exercise, Reading, Scribing (journaling). Spend 5-10 minutes on each. Win the morning, win the day.
source: The Miracle Morning by Hal Elrod

title: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck
summary: The key to a good life is not giving a f*ck about more things - it's giving a f*ck about fewer things, only the ones that truly matter. You can't be happy all the time; pain and uncertainty are part of growth. Choose your struggles wisely. Who you are is defined by what you're willing to struggle for.
source: The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck by Mark Manson

title: Steal Like an Artist
summary: Nothing is original. Every artist steals - the good ones steal well. Start copying your heroes, and in the process, you'll find your own voice. Be boring (have a day job) so you can be creative on your own terms. Creativity is subtraction - constraints breed creativity.
source: Steal Like an Artist by Austin Kleon

title: Daring Greatly
summary: Vulnerability is not winning or losing - it's having the courage to show up when you can't control the outcome. The critic who sneers from the safe sidelines isn't the one whose opinion matters. It's the person in the arena, face marred by dust and sweat and blood, who dares greatly.
source: Daring Greatly by Brené Brown

title: The Power of Full Engagement
summary: Manage your energy, not your time. The human body runs in 90-120 minute ultradian rhythms. Work in focused sprints, then fully disengage. Physical energy (eat, sleep, exercise) is the foundation. Emotional energy comes from positive relationships. Mental from focus. Spiritual from purpose.
source: The Power of Full Engagement by Jim Loehr

title: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman
summary: Richard Feynman approached physics - and life - with relentless curiosity and playfulness. He learned to pick locks, play samba drums, and crack safes at Los Alamos. He refused to take anything on authority. If he couldn't explain it simply, he didn't understand it well enough.
source: Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman by Richard Feynman

title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
summary: Habit 1: Be proactive. Habit 2: Begin with the end in mind. Habit 3: Put first things first. Habit 4: Think win-win. Habit 5: Seek first to understand. Habit 6: Synergize. Habit 7: Sharpen the saw. These principles are timeless and universal - effectiveness comes from character, not technique.
source: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People by Stephen Covey

title: Made to Stick
summary: Why do some ideas survive and others die? The SUCCESs framework: Simple (find the core), Unexpected (grab attention), Concrete (make it tangible), Credible (give proof), Emotional (make people care), Stories (drive action). Urban legends stick because they have all six. Your ideas can too.
source: Made to Stick by Chip & Dan Heath

title: On Writing Well
summary: Writing is hard because rewriting is hard. The secret: cut every word that doesn't do work. Simplify. Strip every sentence to its cleanest components. The reader has an attention span of about 30 seconds - respect that. Good writing comes from rewriting. Style is who you are. Just be clear.
source: On Writing Well by William Zinsser

title: Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me)
summary: Cognitive dissonance is the engine of self-justification. When we do something wrong, we change our beliefs to justify it rather than admit we were wrong. This is how good people do bad things - and convince themselves it was right. Awareness is the only defense.
source: Mistakes Were Made by Tavris & Aronson

title: The Courage to Be Disliked
summary: All problems are interpersonal relationship problems. The fear of being disliked traps you. Freedom is being disliked by other people - that's the price you pay for living your own life. Separate your tasks from others' tasks. The courage to be disliked is the courage to be happy.
source: The Courage to Be Disliked by Kishimi & Koga

title: The Road Less Traveled
summary: Life is difficult. Once you truly accept that, life becomes less difficult. Discipline is the toolset for solving life's problems - delayed gratification, acceptance of responsibility, dedication to truth, and balancing. Love is not a feeling - it's the choice to extend yourself for another's growth.
source: The Road Less Traveled by M. Scott Peck

title: The Third Chimpanzee
summary: Humans share 98.4% of our DNA with chimpanzees. We're the third chimpanzee, after common chimps and bonobos. What makes us different? Language, art, agriculture, and the capacity for genocide. Our big brains let us dominate the planet - and also destroy it.
source: The Third Chimpanzee by Jared Diamond

title: 12 Rules for Life
summary: Rule 1: Stand up straight with your shoulders back. Rule 2: Treat yourself like someone you're responsible for helping. Rule 3: Make friends with people who want the best for you. Order and chaos are the fundamental forces. Meaning comes from taking responsibility beyond yourself.
source: 12 Rules for Life by Jordan Peterson

title: When Breath Becomes Air
summary: At 36, neurosurgeon Paul Kalanithi was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer. He wrote about facing death with honesty, love, and courage. 'The question is not whether we live or die - but how we choose to live while we're alive.' His last words: 'To be willing to be broken by another.'
source: When Breath Becomes Air by Paul Kalanithi

title: The War of Art
summary: Resistance is the enemy of creativity - the invisible force that keeps you from doing your work. It's fear, procrastination, self-doubt, distraction. The only way to beat Resistance is to sit down and do the work. Professional artists show up every day. Amateurs wait for inspiration. Be a professional.
source: The War of Art by Steven Pressfield

title: Wherever You Go, There You Are
summary: Meditation isn't about escaping life - it's about being fully present in it. The only moment you ever have is now. Mindfulness is paying attention, on purpose, without judgment. Stop rushing. Stop multitasking. Sit still for 10 minutes. Enlightenment is showing up for your own life.
source: Wherever You Go, There You Are by Jon Kabat-Zinn
